course.title: Bariatric surgery
course.html:
Obesity

  • BMI
Underweight< 18.5
Normal weight18.5-24.9
Overweight25-29.9 (Grade I)
ObesityObesity≥ 30
Grade II: 30-39.9
Grade III: ≥ 40

Interactions of obesity

RespiratorySleep apnea, higher risk for respiratory infections, bronchial asthma, Pickwickian
syndrome (obesity hypoventilation syndrome)
MalignantAssociated with endometrial, prostate, colon, breast, gallbladder and lung cancer
PsychologicalSocial stigmatization and depression
CardiovascularCAD, essential hypertension, LVH, cor pulmonale, atherosclerosis
CNSStroke, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meralgia paresthetica
SurgicalIncreased surgical risk and post-OP complications including wound infections, post-OP
pneumonia, DVT, pulmonary embolism
PelvicStress incontinence
Obstetric and perinatalPregnancy related hypertension, fetal macrosomia, pelvic dystocia
GIGallbladder disease (cholecystitis, cholelithiasis), NASH, fatty liver, reflux esophagitis
OrthopedicOsteoarthritis, coxa vera, chronic lumbago, Blount and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
MetabolicDM 2, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome, dylipidemia
ReproductiveFEMALE → anovulation, early puberty, infertility, hyperandrogenism, PCOS
MALE → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
CutaneousIntertrigo, acanthosis nigricans, hirsutism, increased risk for cellulitis and carbuncles
ExtremitiesVenous varicosities, lowe extremity venous and/or lymphatic edema
MiscellaneousReduced mobility and difficulty maintaining personal hygiene

Secondary causes of obesity

  • Hypothyroidism
  • Cushing’s syndrome
  • Insulinoma
  • PCOS
  • Genetic syndromes (Prader Willi etc.)
  • GH deficiency
  • Oral contraceptives
  • Pregnancy
  • Hypogonadism
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism
  • Tube feeding related obesity

What to do?

  • 1. Diet
  • 2. Physical activity
  • 3. Behavior modification
  • Food addiction!
  • Psychotherapy
  • Medication
  • Surgery

Bariatric surgery

  • Aimes at decreasing weight of obese patients by performing operations on stomach or small intestine
  • Should be considered as treatment of last resort after dieting, exercise, psychotherapy, drugs have failed

Indication for surgery

  • BMI > 40 kg/m2

Or

  • BMI > 35 kg/m2 in combination with high-risk comorbid conditions (sleep apnea, Pickwickian syndrome, DM1,

degenerative joint disease, dyslipidemia, NASH)

Or

  • BMI 30-35 with at least one of the following: uncontrolled DM2, metabolic syndrome

Contraindications for bariatric surgery

  • Bulimia nervosa
  • Age > 65
  • Pediatric pat. before end of growth
  • Untreated depression
  • Major psychosis
  • Drug and alcohol addiction
  • CV disease with high anesthetic risk, coagulopathies difficult to correct
  • Pregnancy
  • Cirrhosis

Pre-OP preparation

  • Psychological evaluation !
  • Previous weight loss
  • Type of eating mistakes
  • Encourage pat. to begin physical exertion
  • Identify health-related risk behaviors
  • Quit smoking
  • Gastroscopy and H Pylori test
  • Ventilatory test should be performed
  • Cardiac, liver function
  • Doppler if previous DVT or hypercoagulability → Prophylaxis by heparin (LMWH)
  • PPI/ anti H2
  • Single dose AB prophylaxis
  • Calf compression and DVT prophylaxis by administration of low molecular weight heparin

Post-OP

  • Pre-/ peri- and post-OP nutrition program
  • Assessment and improvement of comorbidities (hypertension, DM2, OSA, COPD, malnutrition)
  • Avoidance of pregnancy in first 18-24 months after surgery

Principles of bariatric surgery

  • 1. Capacity reduction of digestive canal which will physically make patient incapable of eating same quantity of food

– Restrictive operations

  • 2. Capacity reduction of digestive canal of absorption of food - Malabsorptive operations
  • 3. Restrictive + malabsorptive operations
  • 1. Restrictive operations
  • → Adjustable gastric banding
    • Silicone plastic ring placed around eso-gastric junction
    • Internal circumference which is inflated with saline (injection port placed subcutaneously in left upper quadrant)
    • Reducing esophageal lumen

Pre-OP

  • Must lose 5-10 kg to reduce glycogen and fat content of liver → lowers volume and liver friability
  • Intake of sufficient amount of quality protein
  • Avoid refined sugars and saturated fats
Contraindications- Pat. unable to comply with dietary restrictions imposed by ring
- Allergy to ring components
- Pat. with infection that may contaminate ring
- Coexistence of diseases with high risk of hemodynamic instability (esophageal
varices, intestinal telangiectasia)
- Pat. with psycho-emotional problems severe enough to affect post-OP follow-up
- Autoimmune diseases affecting esophagus (scleroderma, lupus erythema)
Advantages- Short interval for recovery
- No segment of digestive tract opens or resects
- Anatomy does not change but area of fibrosis appears under ring
- Few long-term complications are not as low as supporters claim
- Good long-term results in terms of weight loss
Complications- Small pouch/ esophageal dilatation
- Digestive hemorrhage
- Esophagitis due to stasis in dilated oesophagus
- Ring slipage
- Gastric stenosis at level of ring
- Infection at port site
- Foul belching
- Fistula between pouch and fundus of stomach
- Intraoperative rupture of ring
- Loss of saline from system

Post-OP care

  • Liquid diet first week
  • Disinfection of skin by applying a swab with antiseptic for 10 minutes before calibration is mandatory
  • Maximum volume that can be injected in ring is 9 ml
  • Each calibration of 0.5-1ml should be spaced by 1-2 months
  • 2. Malabsorptive operations
  • Sleeve gastrectomy (SG) or gastric plication

Sleeve = partial gastrectomy

  • First choice of all options
  • removes most of vertical part of stomach
  • detaching blood supply to larger curvature
  • calibration tube of 32-38 French is slipped in stomach close to lesser curvature
  • using linear cutter 70% of stomach is removed beginning from antrum and progressing upwards to Hiss angle

Plication = 2 layers which folds greater curvature into lumen of stomach

  • first week vomiting is quite frequent
  • stomach dilates after 2-3 years and most of patients regain weight close
  • operation is reversible for 1-2 weeks then adhesions become dense and almost irreversible
  • patient profile: young female, moderate obesity, single, with intensive support from entourage, able to play sports and willing to change their eating habits
  • Both cause limits food intake due to
  • Reduced gastric reservoir (remaining tube 100 ml) and early satiety
  • Reducing hunger (↓ ghrelin production from gastric wall)
  • Advantage: does not require foreign materials

Indication

  • Primary operation for obesity, especially in patients with type 2 diabetes
  • Bridging to gastric bypass
  • Replacement of adjustable ring (2 steps necessary)
  • Suitable for ages under 14 or over 70

Pre-OP care

  • Weight loss in order to reduce volume of frail fatty liver
  • High protein intake
  • Avoid sugar and saturated fat
  • Vitamins and protein shakes 10 days pre-operatively

Post-OP care

  • First 10 days only liquid diet
  • 2nd post-OP day methylene blue given to detect fistulas (can appear after 2 weeks and become symptomatic even

at 1 month)

  • On day 6. advisable to administer water-soluble iodinated contrast agent to highlight any fistulas
  • Resumption of diet: soups - mashed items - cream soup - diluted yogurts - mashed meat
  • Feeding is resumed progressively in a manner similar for infants
  • Food discipline - no carbonated drinks, avoiding high calorie food
  • Adequate fluid intake very important to avoid dehydration and hemoconcentration (risk of portal thrombosis)

Outpatient care

  • Prolonged mastication
  • Stop eating when satiety or regurgitation occurs
  • Adequate fractionated fluid intake
  • Avoid drinking during meals, 15 min before and 30 after
  • iv infusion if on 2 consecutive days an intake of 1500 ml is not possible
  • Progressive testing for tolerance
  • Progressive increase volume of physical activity

Complications (rare but can lead to death)

  • Bleeding
  • Stapling line fistulas, appear especially immediately subcardially and can be difficult to treat
  • Marginal ulcers of gastric tube, due to ischemic disorders
  • SG has higher incidence of postoperative gastroesophageal reflux disease due to gastric tube in which endoluminal

pressure is increased

  • Megaloblastic anemia due to lack of intrinsic factor (produced by stomach, requires vitamin B12) → necessary to

supplement Vit. B12

  • 3. Restrictive and malabsorption surgeries
  • Gastric bypass (short Roux-en-Y or long Roux-en-Y
  • Duodenal switch
  • BMI > 40 or
  • BMI of 35 with obesity related illness (DM2, CHD, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis)

! Followed by major disorders and were abandoned

Which procedure?

  • Sweet eater → gastric bypass
  • Volume eater → sleeve gastrectomy, duodenal switch
  • Addiction to food → duodenal switch

Procedure

  • combines gastric restriction with malabsorption
  • 50 ml gastric pouch obtained by transecting in transverse fashion stomach at 3 cm under esogastric junction, without removing distal part
  • malabsorbtion ensured by Y jejunal loop with biliary limb much longer than usually (200 cm)
  • patients require lifelong dietary and vitamin supplements and need to be followed by multidisciplinary team

Post-OP care

  • Eating
  • 1. First days: clear liquid diet → clear broth, diluted fruit juices or sugar-free gelatin desserts
  • 2. Blended or puréed sugar-free diet for at least two weeks
  • 3. Diet that is relatively high in protein and low in fats and alcohol
  • 4. Daily multivitamin pill for life to compensate for reduced absorption of essential nutrients

Weight loss in first 10 months

  • Biliopancreatic diversion → 53kg
  • Roux-en-Y gastric bypass → 41kg
  • Open → 43kg
  • Laparoscopic → 38kg
  • Vertical banded gastroplasty → 32kg

book.html:
Bariatric surgery

Ion Cosmin Puia

Obesity affects up to a third of the population of some countries and has a growing trend. Unfortunately even a higher percentage is registered in children. Diets have a limited efficiency and are usually followed by a relapse.Several health problems are associated with obesity:

  • diabetes
  • gallstones
  • hypertension
  • chronic lung diseases
  • hypertension
  • sleep apnea
  • degenerative diseases of the spine, knees and hips
  • social integration and psychosocial difficulties.

Bariatric or metabolic surgery, as it is called now, aimes at decreasing the weight of obese patients by performing operations on the stomach or small intestine. There are restrictive ones, which prevent the patient to consume large amounts of food and malabsorptive, which reduce the absorption surface. The first category includes adjustable gastric band, gastric sleeve and gastric plication. Pure malabsorptive interventions are followed by major disorders and were abandoned. Gastric bypass combines gastric restriction with malabsorption. A 50ml gastric pouch is obtained by transecting in a transverse fashion the stomach at 3 cm under the esogastric junction, without removing the distal part. The malabsorbtion is ensured by a Y jejunal loop with the biliary limb much longer than usually (200 cm). These patients require life long dietary and vitamin supplements and need to be followed by a multidisciplinary team.

Patients’ main selection criterion for bariatric surgery is BMI over 40 kg / m² or 35 if there is at least a comorbidity that can be positively influenced by weight loss.

Improvements are recorded in most comorbidities:

  • Diabetes, especially type II ( indication even at BMI 29)
  • Sleep apnea (+ snoring )
  • HTA
  • Arthrosis
  • Lower limb edema
  • GERD
  • Amenorrhea
  • Dyslipidemia

Contraindications for metabolic surgery :

  • depression
  • drug or alcohol abuse
  • pregnancy
  • cirrhosis

Preoperative preparation:

  • quit smoching
  • psychological assessment
  • asessment by a specialist in eating disorders
  • gastroscopy and H Pylori test
  • pulmonary function test (breathing test)
  • cardiological assessment.

Preoperative measures:

  • deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis by administration of heparin

derivatives with low molecular weight

  • PPI or anti H2
  • single dose of prophylactic antibiotic
  • apply sequential calf compression and graduated compression

stockings.

Adjustable gastric band -is made of silicone plastic and has a tube on the internal circumference which is inflated with saline (maximum 9ml), thus reducing the oesophageal lumen. It communicates by a thin tube with an injection port placed subcutaneously in the left upper quadrant. By injecting saline solution in the port the oesophageal lumen will be diminished and thus food intake will be limited. The ring is placed around the esogastric junction.

Advantages of the adjustable gastric band:

  • no segment of the digestive tract is opened or resected
  • short recovery
  • low incidence of complications

Specific contraindications:

  • patients unable respect the food intake restrictions imposed by the ring
  • allergy to the ring components
  • patients with an infection that is likely to contaminate the ring
  • patients with severe psycho-emotional problems

Postoperative care:

  • liquid diet the first week

Disinfection of the skin by applying a swab with antiseptic for 10 minutes before the calibration is mandatory.

The maximum volume that can be injected in the ring is 9 ml. Each calibration of 0.5-1ml should be spaced by 1-2 months.

Complications:

  • oesophageal dilation
  • oesophagitis due to stasis in a dilated oesophagus
  • ring slipage
  • gastric stenosis at the level of the ring
  • infection at the port site
  • foul belching
  • fistula between pouch and fundus of the stomach
  • intraoperative rupture of the ring
  • injection in the tube (loss of saline from the system).

Sleeve gastrectomy -has replaced the adjustable ring as the first option for bariatric surgery. The operation removes most of the vertical part of the stomach. It begins by detaching the blood supply to the larger curvature. A calibration tube of 32-38 French is slipped in the stomach close to the lesser curvature. By using a linear cutter 70% of the stomach is removed beginning from the antrum and progressing upwards to the Hiss angle.

Preoperative preparation:

  • weight loss in order to reduce the volume of a frail fatty liver
  • high protein intake
  • avoid sugar and saturated fat
  • vitamins and protein shakes 10 days preoperatively.

Sleeve gastrectomy effectiveness in the treatment of morbid obesity is caused by several mechanisms that limit food intake:

  • reducing hunger by lowering the plasmatic level of ghrelin ("hunger" hormone
  • installing early satiety (the fast filling of the vertical segement of the stomach increases intraluminal pressure)

An important advantage of the sleeve gastrectomy is that it does not require the use of foreign materials.

Indications:

  • primary operation for obesity, especially in patients with type 2 diabetes
  • bridging to gastric bypass
  • replacement of adjustable ring ( two steps necessary)
  • suitable for ages under 14 or over 70.

The complications are rare (1-3%):

  • Bleeding
  • Fistula suture line
  • Marginal ulcers

Postoperative care:

  • first 10 days liquid intake
  • 2nd postoperative day methylene blue ingestion to check for a fistula
  • day 6: iodine contrast media swallow (fistula?)
  • total oral rehydration is usually possible from PO day 5
  • feeding is resumed progressively in a manner similar for infants
  • food discipline - no carbonated drinks, avoiding high calorie food
  • megaloblastic anemia due to lack of intrinsic factor (produced by the stomach) requires vitamin B12.

Outpatient care:

  • thorough mastication
  • regurgitation equals hasty or too large meals
  • adequate and fractionated fluid intake is the best prophylaxis for portal thrombosis
  • iv infusion if on two consecutive days an intake of 1500ml is not possible
  • avoid drinking while eating

The average excess weight loss is variable:

  • 40% at 6 months
  • 60% to 12
  • 7% to 24 months.

A slight regain after 18 months is possible.

Gastric plication -consists of 2 layers which folds the greater curvature into the lumen of the stomach.

The first week vomiting is quite frequent. The stomach dilates after 2-3 years and most of the patients regain weight close to the initial value.

The operation is reversible for 1-2 weeks then the adhesions become dense and almost irreversible so the conversion to sleeve is very difficult.

The patient profile recommendable for plication is: young female, with moderate obesity, single, with intensive support from the entourage, able to play sports and willing to change their eating habits.
